cues.text: Let us turn now to a topic that decides whether many digital transformation efforts succeed or fail: managing resistance.
Start with a simple question.
Why do people resist change?
When an organisation introduces new software, new processes or new ways of working, some people push back.
The source gives us a list of the common causes, and it is worth taking each one seriously.
First, fear of job loss.
If employees believe that automation or a new system could make their work unnecessary, they will naturally be anxious.
Second, uncertain roles.
Even when jobs are safe, people may not know what their responsibilities will be once the change arrives.
Third, limited skills.
A person who does not feel capable of using a new tool may resist it to avoid looking incompetent.
Fourth, unclear vision.
If nobody explains where the organisation is going and why, the change feels arbitrary.
Fifth, lack of trust.
If staff do not trust management, they will doubt its promises about the change.
Sixth, poorly designed systems.
Sometimes the technology itself is hard to use, slow or badly matched to the work.
Seventh, past failures.
If earlier initiatives collapsed or were abandoned, people reasonably expect the same to happen again.
Eighth, change fatigue.
When changes arrive one after another with no time to settle, people become exhausted and stop engaging.
And ninth, infrastructure barriers, such as unreliable connectivity, unstable power or inadequate devices, which make it genuinely hard to use the new system, however willing the person is.
Now comes the most important idea in this block: resistance is information, not automatically employee stubbornness.
This changes how a leader should respond.

Instead of asking, "How do I get these people to comply?", a good leader asks, "What is this resistance telling me?" The source tells us to investigate whether objections reveal genuine operational or customer risks.
For example, if staff say a new process will slow down service, they may be right, and ignoring them could harm customers.
Resistance can be an early warning system.
Next, the source offers strategies for managing resistance.
There are six, and I will take them in order.
The first strategy: communicate the reason, expected benefits, changes and uncertainties honestly.
Notice the word honestly, and notice that uncertainties are included.
Leaders should not pretend to know everything.
Admitting what is not yet decided builds trust, while overpromising destroys it.
The second strategy: involve employees and customers in design, and use pilots and feedback.
People support what they help create.
Pilots are small-scale trials that let the organisation test a change, gather feedback and correct problems before wider rollout.
The third strategy: offer role-specific training, coaching, accessible materials and support.
Role-specific means that a cashier, a manager and an analyst each receive training matched to what they actually do, not one generic session for everybody.
Coaching gives personal guidance, and accessible materials mean people can learn in formats and at times that suit them.
Support must continue after the training ends.
The fourth strategy: appoint change champions, secure visible leadership sponsorship and recognise contributions.
Change champions are respected colleagues who help peers adopt the change.
Visible leadership sponsorship means senior leaders openly back the effort, not just in name.
And recognising contributions rewards people who help the change succeed.
The fifth strategy: remove structural barriers, adjust workflows and incentives, and manage workload and expectations.
This is a powerful point.
If the organisation's rules, targets or reward systems still encourage the old way of working, people will rationally keep to the old way.
Workflows must be redesigned, incentives aligned, and workload managed so that people are not asked to do their old job and learn the new one at full pace at the same time.
The sixth strategy: measure adoption, capability and outcomes, and revise where users struggle.
Three things are measured here.
Adoption asks whether people are actually using the system.
Capability asks whether they can use it well.
Outcomes ask whether the change is delivering the intended results.
And when users struggle, the organisation should revise its approach rather than blame them.
Now consider the practical example the source gives.
A staff member keeps using manual records despite new software being available.
It is tempting to call this laziness.
But the source says the person may face connectivity problems or missing functionality.
In other words, the manual record may be the only thing that works for them.

In many settings, including parts of Nigeria and elsewhere in Africa where connectivity can be inconsistent, this is a realistic concern, though the source itself does not name a specific country here.
The correct response is to diagnose with interviews, observation and usage data before imposing sanctions.
Interviews let you hear the person's explanation.
Observation lets you see the work as it happens.
Usage data shows patterns in how and when the system is used.
Only after diagnosing the cause should the organisation decide what to do.
Finally, the source discusses rollout approaches.
A gradual rollout introduces the change in stages, which allows learning.
Problems found early can be fixed before they affect everyone.
A big-bang rollout switches everyone at once.
The source notes that some dependencies may require a big-bang rollout, for example when systems are so interconnected that they cannot run in two versions.
But it creates concentrated risk, because if something goes wrong, it goes wrong everywhere at the same time.
There is also a third option: parallel operation, where the old and new systems run side by side.
The source gives a firm condition.
Use parallel operation only with a clear authoritative record and a reconciliation plan.
An authoritative record means everyone knows which system holds the official truth.
A reconciliation plan means there is a defined process for comparing the two and resolving differences.
Without these, parallel running produces duplicated work and conflicting data, and nobody knows which version to trust.

To bring it together: resistance has many causes, it carries useful information, and it is best managed through honest communication, involvement, training, visible sponsorship, removal of structural barriers, and careful measurement, with a rollout approach chosen deliberately according to its risks.
